## Worldview
Medicine follows Galen and Avicenna as taught at Bologna, Padua and Montpellier: disease is an imbalance of the four humours; pestilence comes from corrupted air (miasma) stirred up by planetary conjunctions, earthquakes and God's anger at sin. Natural philosophy is scholastic Aristotle. Astrology is respected science. There is no printing: knowledge travels by sermon, council decree, notary, letter and copyist, and most people cannot read Latin. Florence is a guild republic of perhaps 90,000 to 100,000 people, governed since 1343 by priors drawn by lot from the guilds, shaken by the collapse of the Bardi and Peruzzi banks and by the famine of 1346–47. The pope sits at Avignon. Practical knowledge lives in workshops and guilds; merchants reckon with Arabic numerals in abacus schools but keep formal ledgers in Roman numerals.

## People
- **Gentile da Foligno**: Professor of medicine at Perugia, the most respected physician in central Italy. Knows: Avicenna's Canon; writes plague consilia for Genoa (late 1347 or early 1348), Perugia and Pisa (poisonous corrupted air, contagion, theriac, bleeding, fires, avoidance of the sick). — At Perugia in 1347, three or four days' ride from Florence. Dies of plague near Foligno on 18 June 1348 after tending the sick.
- **Tommaso del Garbo**: Florentine physician, son of the physician Dino del Garbo; professor at Perugia and Bologna. Knows: Galenic and Avicennan medicine; author of a vernacular Consiglio contro a pistolenza with practical household advice (airing rooms, vinegar, keeping distance from the sick). — Where he is in autumn 1347 is not certain (Florence, Perugia or Bologna). Survives the plague; dies 1370.
- **Giovanni Villani**: Merchant, former mint and grain official, chronicler. Knows: The city's numbers (baptisms, mouths, schools, hospitals, wool output), the 1333 flood, the famine of 1346–47, the bank failures, astrology of calamities. — In Florence, ruined by the Buonaccorsi failure and jailed for it in the Stinche in 1346. Dies in the plague in 1348, leaving the chronicle unfinished.
- **Matteo Villani**: Giovanni's brother, merchant. Knows: Commerce and city politics; continues the chronicle and describes the plague and its aftermath. — In Florence; survives 1348 and dies in the plague of 1363.
- **Giovanni Boccaccio**: Writer, son of the merchant Boccaccino di Chellino. Knows: Naples and its court, Latin letters, the merchant world; later describes the plague in Florence in the Decameron. — Probably at Forlì or Ravenna in 1347; whether he witnessed the Florentine plague himself is debated. His father dies in 1349.
- **Guy de Chauliac**: Surgeon and physician to Pope Clement VI. Knows: Surgery, anatomy from Bologna and Montpellier; in 1348 distinguishes a first form with fever and blood-spitting from a later form with buboes. — At Avignon. Stays at his post in 1348, falls ill with a bubo and survives.
- **Angelo Acciaiuoli**: Dominican, bishop of Florence (1342–1355). Knows: The clergy, preaching and processions, which are how instructions reach the whole city without print. — In Florence; a leader of the 1343 rising against the Duke of Athens. Survives the plague.
- **Francesco Balducci Pegolotti**: Former factor of the Bardi company, author of the merchant handbook Pratica della mercatura. Knows: Trade routes to Tana and Cathay, spices, alum, soap, sugar grades, assaying and refining of gold and silver. — In Florence in 1347, occupied with the liquidation of the Bardi company. Date of death unknown.
- **Paolo dell'Abbaco (Paolo Dagomari)**: abacus master, astronomer and astrologer. Knows: commercial arithmetic, algebra in words, root extraction, astronomical tables and almanacs. — About 65, teaches at his school by Santa Trinita in Florence; the best-known reckoner in the city. Survives the plague and dies in 1374.
- **Jacopo Dondi**: physician and astronomer in Padua. Knows: the astronomical tower clock set up in Padua in 1344, astronomical tables, tides. — In Padua, about a week's journey from Florence. Dies in 1359.
- **Giovanni Dondi**: student of medicine and astronomy, Jacopo's son. Knows: clockwork and planetary theory; begins his astrarium, a geared planetary clock, in 1348. — About seventeen, in Padua. Survives the plague; finishes the astrarium in 1364.
- **Jean Buridan**: master of arts at the university of Paris. Knows: impetus, logic of consequences, questions on Aristotle's physics. — In Paris, weeks away; reachable by letter in Latin through friars or merchants. Survives the plague.
- **Thomas Bradwardine**: Oxford mathematician and theologian, royal chaplain. Knows: proportions of speeds, the Merton school's arithmetic of motion. — With Edward III in France and England. Becomes archbishop of Canterbury in 1349 and dies of the plague that August.
- **Jean de Murs**: astronomer, mathematician and music theorist in Paris. Knows: Alfonsine Tables, eclipse computation, calendar reform, arithmetic and algebra. — In Paris; advised Clement VI at Avignon on the calendar in 1344-1345. Alive into the 1350s.
- **Andrea Pisano**: sculptor, goldsmith and master builder. Knows: bronze door casting, the campanile works, stone hoisting. — Made the Baptistery's bronze doors (1330-1336); by 1347 master of works at Orvieto cathedral. Dies about 1348-1349.
- **Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)**: poet and scholar, crowned in Rome 1341, son of a Florentine exile. Knows: Cicero, Livy, manuscript hunting, the papal court. — At Avignon and Vaucluse until November 1347, then Parma and Verona. Has never lived in Florence (first visit 1350). Survives; his Laura dies at Avignon in April 1348.
- **Clement VI (Pierre Roger)**: pope at Avignon since 1342. Knows: theology, diplomacy, patronage of scholars and physicians. — At Avignon, some weeks' journey away. In July and September 1348 issues bulls forbidding attacks on Jews over the plague. Survives.
- **Bartolus of Sassoferrato**: professor of civil law. Knows: Roman law, city statutes, the legal standing of free cities. — Teaching at Perugia since 1343. Survives the plague; dies 1357.
- **Werner of Urslingen**: German mercenary captain, leader of the Great Company. Knows: cavalry warfare, extortion by contract. — Plundered Tuscany in 1342; in 1347–48 serves Louis of Hungary's invasion of Naples.
- **Cola di Rienzo**: notary, tribune of Rome from May 1347. Knows: Roman antiquities and inscriptions, popular oratory. — Rules Rome May–December 1347 and writes to Florence for support; flees in December.

## Events and timeline
- 1346 Jan: the Bardi company fails (January 1345 in Florentine reckoning), after the Peruzzi (1343); credit and employment in the city collapse.
- 1346: plague breaks out in the Mongol army besieging Genoese Caffa in the Crimea.
- 1346 Mar: the Franciscan inquisitor Piero dell'Aquila, collecting a cardinal's debt from the failed Acciaiuoli, has citizens seized; a crowd frees one. He excommunicates the priors and lays an interdict; the commune curbs his powers and the clergy's armed retinues.
- 1346 Aug 26: Crécy. English archers and dismounted men-at-arms defeat French cavalry and Genoese crossbowmen; Villani reports English bombards.
- 1346 Sep–1347 Aug: Edward III besieges Calais for eleven months; it surrenders from hunger.
- 1346 autumn: harvest fails across Tuscany after months of rain.
- 1347 Feb: Genoa founds the Maona of Chios, repaying the shipowners of its 1346 fleet with shares in the island's revenues.
- 1347 Apr: William of Ockham dies at Munich.
- 1347 mid-Apr: famine at its worst. The commune bakes bread in its own ovens and rations it by ticket, two loaves a mouth; Villani counts 94,000 mouths.
- 1347 May 20: Cola di Rienzo seizes power in Rome as tribune; he abdicates and flees on Dec 15.
- 1347 summer: sickness follows the famine; Villani reports more than 4,000 dead in Florence, mostly women and children.
- 1347 Aug: the commune issues a new, worse silver coin, the guelfo of five soldi; a comet is seen, which Villani records as a sign.
- 1347 early Oct: Genoese galleys from the Black Sea bring the plague to Messina.
- 1347 Oct 11: Emperor Ludwig of Bavaria dies excommunicate; the pope's candidate Charles IV is left as king.
- 1347 Oct 23: date of the oldest surviving premium insurance contract, drawn by a Genoese notary.
- 1347 autumn: rumours of the sickness reach Florence with merchants' letters; the commune takes first precautions.
- 1347 Nov: Petrarch leaves Avignon for Italy. Louis of Hungary marches through Italy toward Naples; Queen Joanna flees to Provence.
- 1347 Nov–Dec: plague in Sardinia, Corsica and Marseille.
- 1347 Nov 25: Nicholas of Autrecourt recants and burns his writings in Paris.
- 1348 Jan: plague at Genoa and Pisa (carried to Pisa by galleys), soon after at Venice. Louis of Hungary enters Naples. Jan 25: great earthquake in Friuli and Carinthia, felt across northern Italy and read as a sign; the last event in Villani's chronicle.
- 1348 early: Florence has the streets cleaned, refuses entry to the sick and holds processions (Boccaccio).
- 1348 Mar: first plague deaths in Florence. Mar 30: Venice appoints three citizens as a temporary health commission.
- 1348 Apr: Florence gives a temporary commission of eight citizens special powers over cleaning, removal of the sick and infected goods, and burials.
- 1348 May 2: Pistoia issues plague ordinances: no travel to or from Pisa and Lucca, no imported cloth, deep graves, limits on funerals, rules for butchers.
- 1348 May–Jul: the plague peaks in Florence; perhaps half the city dies. Shops and courts close, the rich flee to their villas, the dead go into layered trench graves (Stefani). Giovanni Villani dies, and the painters Bernardo Daddi in Florence and probably the Lorenzetti brothers in Siena.
- 1348 Jun 9: Queen Joanna sells Avignon to Clement VI.
- 1348 Jun 18: Gentile da Foligno dies of plague near Foligno.
- 1348 Jul 6 and Sep 26: Clement VI's bulls declare the charge that Jews cause the plague false and forbid harming them; massacres nonetheless spread from Provence and Savoy into the Empire that autumn.
- 1348 late summer–autumn: the plague ebbs in Florence. The Company of Orsanmichele is left some 350,000 florins by the dying (Matteo Villani). The commune resolves to found a university (Studio); the papal charter follows in May 1349.
- 1348 Oct: the Paris medical faculty delivers its Compendium de epidemia to King Philip VI: the cause is the conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in Aquarius on 20 March 1345, corrupting the air.
- 1348: Giovanni Dondi begins the astrarium in Padua (finished 1364).

## Quest hooks
- Ride to Perugia before winter and argue with Gentile da Foligno; his consilium will be copied across Italy, so whatever he writes about clothing, bedding and the sickroom will travel further than any sermon.
- Persuade the priors to make the gate officials hold back cloth, bedding and travellers from Pisa for a fixed number of days, against the wool guild and a city still hungry from the famine.
- Get Giovanni Villani, bankrupt and bitter, and the parish gravediggers to tally deaths by parish and week, the first such count in the city, and keep the tally going if Villani dies himself.
- The grain at Orsanmichele is full of rats. Rat-proofing the stores can be sold to the grain officials as saving bread, with no theory of plague needed.
- A physician reports that patients who cough blood die within three days and so do those who nursed them, while bubo patients' nurses sometimes live. What does the player make of it, and who will listen?
- Without print, an instruction reaches the city only through the bishop's preachers, the guild consuls, notaries and criers. Each channel wants something in return.
- A Dominican preacher will carry any message to thousands, if it can be squared with scripture and Galen.
- Rumours of poisoned wells arrive from across the Alps. Anything the player has said about invisible things in water may be turned against the city's few Jews or against strangers.
- Florence has no public clock. The Signoria would pay for one on the tower of the Palazzo dei Priori; the nearest people who understand an escapement are the Dondi in Padua.
- Paolo dell'Abbaco can turn a rule into a table faster than anyone in the city. Win him and logarithms, decimal fractions or a count of the dead become possible.
- A physician's water-filled urine flask in a sunbeam shows that colours come out of white light. The Dominicans know Theodoric's rainbow and will argue.
- The mint tests florins by touchstone and fire. Weighing a coin in air and in water would catch false gold without destroying it.
- Spectacle makers grind only convex lenses. The first concave pair lets a short-sighted prior or banker see across the piazza.
- For the Baptistery doors Florence had to fetch a founder from Venice. Anything in cast bronze larger than a bell needs outside help or patient trials.
- A letter to Buridan in Paris on falling and thrown bodies would reach the one man in Europe already halfway there.
- Creditors of a failed company fight over ledgers at the Mercanzia; an honest reckoning would be worth a patron.
- A merchant back from Caffa or Tana tells what he saw of the sickness in the East.
- The grain officials must feed 94,000 mouths again and suspect the bakers' count.
- Holders of Monte credits want to know what a promise of the commune is worth.
- The commune hears a free company is coming south with the Hungarian army and must choose between paying it off and manning the walls.
- A cartolaio with ten copyists cannot fill an order; he would listen to any way of making books faster.
- A journey to Avignon to reach Clement VI's court before the plague does.
- A copy of the Florentine merchants' letter from Seville about the Canaries voyage of 1341, which Boccaccio put into Latin, is passed round; it tells of islands out in the Ocean.
